PremiseCheck: Efficient Fact-Checking of Human and AI Peer Reviews

Dingjie Song Affiliation: Lehigh University    Zhiling Yan Affiliation: Lehigh University    Ziqian Zhang Affiliation: Lehigh University    Yuxuan Zhang Affiliation: University of British Columbia Affiliation: Vector Institute    Lichao Sun Affiliation: Lehigh University Corresponding author
Abstract

Peer review is under strain from the growth of submissions, and review comments written by humans or AI can misstate what a paper says. We introduce ReviewFact, a benchmark that labels such factual errors in review comments under one definition across NLP, machine learning, and the natural sciences, and that measures cost and latency alongside accuracy. A frontier LLM checks comments well but must read the whole paper for each check, while cheap decision models, which score whether a statement holds in a text, fall far short on whole comments that mix several implicit assertions. PremiseCheck is a framework that combines the two. An LLM rewrites each comment as explicit premises without reading the paper, and a decision model checks each premise against the paper. When each comment is checked on its own, PremiseCheck reaches accuracy comparable to GPT-5.5 across all three fields at about half its cost, and on NLP reviews at a quarter of its cost and less than half its latency.

††Code: https://github.com/OpenLAIR/PremiseCheck††Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/songdj/ReviewFact††Website: https://openlair.github.io/premisecheck/

1 Introduction

The number of research papers has grown explosively in recent years, and reviewing them now places a heavy burden on the scientific community (Shah, 2022; Kuznetsov et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2025). A review comment is useful only if what it says about the paper is true, yet factual errors appear regularly in both human-written and AI-written comments (Du et al., 2024; Ryu et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026), and AI systems now help write a growing share of reviews (Liang et al., 2024a; Thakkar et al., 2025; Biswas et al., 2026). Such errors mislead authors and distort decisions, and at the present scale they can no longer be caught by hand. An area chair cannot reread each paper to check every comment, and an author can correct an error only in the rebuttal.

We therefore study the fact-checking of review comments as a task of its own. Given a paper and one comment from a review of it, a system scores how likely the comment says something that the paper does not support. Errors of judgment, such as whether a concern matters, are out of scope. Existing expert annotations of review comments label factual errors inconsistently, if at all. Our benchmark, ReviewFact, builds on them (Du et al., 2024; Ryu et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026) and labels every comment under one definition of factual error. Because a system would run on every comment of every review, ReviewFact evaluates cost and latency together with accuracy. The task is hard because each error is something an expert reviewer overlooked or misread, and the evidence against it may lie anywhere in a long paper. A comment also rarely states its claim directly, as a question such as “Did the authors test other models?” presupposes that the paper does not test them.

When each comment is checked on its own, existing systems are either accurate or cheap, but not both. A frontier LLM that judges each comment on its own (Zheng et al., 2023; Ryu et al., 2025; Thakkar et al., 2025) must reread the full paper for every comment, a cost that multiplies across tens of thousands of reviews. Instead of generating text, a decision model such as Jev returns the probability that a statement holds in a document, typically within a fraction of a second and at negligible cost (Almeida, 2026; TypeSafe AI, 2026). Yet on whole comments, Jev performs at chance level on the NLP reviews and well below an LLM on the other two parts. A review comment mixes several assertions, many implicit, whereas a decision model, like single-claim fact-checkers (Laban et al., 2022; Zha et al., 2023; Tang et al., 2024), is reliable only on explicit, self-contained claims. On single premises that human annotators wrote out from review comments, however, Jev is as accurate as GPT-5.5 (Appendix D.1). Our key insight is that understanding what a comment asserts needs an LLM but not the paper, whereas reading the paper is the expensive part and a decision model can do it once the assertions are explicit.

PremiseCheck is a framework that combines the two kinds of models. An LLM rewrites each comment as a few explicit premises without reading the paper (Min et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2024; Ryu et al., 2025). A decision model then decides how to check each premise and verifies it against the paper, and the comment receives the score of its weakest premise. Figure 1 contrasts PremiseCheck with either kind of model alone. With a medium-reasoning decomposer, PremiseCheck stays within 0.3 AUROC points of holistic GPT-5.5 or above it on every part of ReviewFact at about half its cost, and on the NLP reviews a decomposer without reasoning cuts the cost to a quarter while remaining non-inferior. The accuracy comes from decomposition rather than from one model, since four decision models from different providers, including the open-weight Kev-27B, come within one point of holistic GPT-5.5 as verifiers.

Our contributions are as follows.

  • •

    We propose PremiseCheck, a framework that turns the verification of a review comment into decision problems, combining the flexibility of an LLM with the efficiency of a decision model. A decision model checks each premise against the paper or against general knowledge and asks several phrasings of its question in one call.

  • •

    We define the task of fact-checking single review comments and build ReviewFact, a benchmark that labels factual errors in human-written and AI-written review comments across NLP, machine learning, and the natural sciences and measures cost and latency alongside accuracy. ReviewFact holds 9,267 comments on 217 papers.

  • •

    We validate PremiseCheck on all three parts of ReviewFact, where it checks each comment on its own with accuracy comparable to GPT-5.5 at a fraction of its cost. A cascade costs more than PremiseCheck yet is less accurate on every part.

2 Related Work

2.1 Factual Errors in Review Comments

As LLMs write reviews and critique human ones (Liang et al., 2024b; D’Arcy et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2025; Thakkar et al., 2025; Zhuang et al., 2025), checking what a review says about a paper matters more. Unlike benchmarks of errors in papers (Son et al., 2025; Zhang and Abernethy, 2025), ReviewCritique (Du et al., 2024), ReviewScore (Ryu et al., 2025), Phys. Rev. B (Kim et al., 2026), and ClaimCheck (Ou et al., 2025) annotate review comments against the paper. These datasets serve broader goals and label factual errors inconsistently, if at all, whereas ReviewFact applies one definition across three fields and also scores cost and latency. Systems that generate reviews aim to write better comments, whereas PremiseCheck checks comments that have already been written.

2.2 Claim Decomposition and Grounded Checking

Fact verification commonly splits a text into atomic claims and checks each one against a source (Min et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2024), often with a small trained fact-checking model (Tang et al., 2024). ReviewScore and Peerispect (Ghorbanpour et al., 2026) bring this recipe to peer review with an LLM as the verifier. When an LLM reads the paper to verify each premise, decomposition multiplies the number of expensive calls instead of reducing it. PremiseCheck instead has an LLM write premises without reading the paper and a decision model check them. Unlike a trained fact-checking model, a decision model such as Jev (Almeida, 2026; TypeSafe AI, 2026) takes a question as input, so PremiseCheck can route each premise and phrase its check in several ways.

2.3 Cost-Aware Inference

Cascades and routers send each query to a cheap or an expensive LLM (Chen et al., 2024; Ong et al., 2025; Dekoninck et al., 2025; Jung et al., 2025), and compound AI systems and agents are now optimized and evaluated for cost (Zaharia et al., 2024; Khattab et al., 2024; Kapoor et al., 2025; Erol et al., 2026). Test-time scaling instead spends more output tokens and time to gain accuracy (Wang et al., 2023; Snell et al., 2025). Unlike a cascade, which still sends most comments and their papers to an expensive LLM, PremiseCheck gives the paper only to the decision model. PremiseCheck also runs counter to test-time scaling, since its decomposer needs no reasoning.

3 The ReviewFact Benchmark

3.1 Task

Given a paper DD and one comment cc from a review of DD, a system outputs a score s⁡(c,D)∈[0,1]s(c,D)\in[0,1], written s⁡(c)s(c) for short, where a low score means that cc likely contains a factual error about DD. A comment contains a factual error when it says something about the paper that the paper does not support. We adopt the set 𝒯\mathcal{T} of four types of factual error of ReviewCritique (Du et al., 2024), in which the comment misreads the paper (Misunderstanding), claims that the paper lacks something it contains (Neglect), asserts something with no basis in the paper (Unstated statement), or misstates its content (Inaccurate summary). Errors of judgment, such as whether a concern is important, are outside the task. Figure 2a shows the task on a real comment.

A dataset for the task is a set of labeled comments 𝒟={(Dj,cj,yj)}j=1N\mathcal{D}=\{(D_{j},c_{j},y_{j})\}_{j=1}^{N}, where yj=1y_{j}=1 if comment cjc_{j} contains a factual error about paper DjD_{j} and yj=0y_{j}=0 otherwise. When the source annotations provide it, an error also has a type tj∈𝒯t_{j}\in\mathcal{T}. Systems are evaluated by AUROC with factual errors as the class to detect,

AUROC=Pr[s(c+)<s(c−)],\mathrm{AUROC}=\Pr\big[s(c^{+})<s(c^{-})\big], (1)

where c+c^{+} is a random comment with y=1y=1, c−c^{-} a random comment with y=0y=0, and ties count one half. We report AUROC multiplied by 100. Because a system runs on every comment, we also measure its cost C⁡(c)C(c) in US dollars and its latency T⁡(c)T(c) in seconds per comment, and we report their means relative to the reference system of §5.

3.2 Labels from Expert Annotations

ReviewFact adds no new comments or papers. It reuses expert judgments of review comments from one dataset per field, ReviewCritique for NLP, ReviewScore for machine learning, and Phys. Rev. B for the natural sciences (Du et al., 2024; Ryu et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026). Human reviewers wrote comments in all three parts, which we call the NLP, machine learning, and natural-science reviews, and AI reviewers also wrote comments in the NLP and natural-science reviews. Each dataset was built for a broader goal, so we map its annotations to our label and leave out comments outside the task, following the rules in Appendix A.1. Figure 2b outlines this process. Figure 4 shows a labeled sample.

Human verification.

Many comments that the Phys. Rev. B experts judged incorrect are errors of judgment rather than factual errors, so GPT-5.5 decides from the expert’s rationale whether the error is factual. Two of the authors independently repeat this decision on the 178 comments that have a rationale, without seeing the GPT-5.5 labels or each other’s labels (Appendix A.2). The two annotators agree with a Cohen’s κ\kappa of 0.70, and GPT-5.5 agrees with them with κ\kappa of 0.76 and 0.77, so we keep the GPT-5.5 labels. With the labels of the annotators instead, the difference between PremiseCheck and holistic GPT-5.5 on these reviews ranges from −3.7-3.7 to +2.7+2.7 and is never significant, so the GPT-5.5 labels do not favor the GPT-5.5 reference.

3.3 Statistics

Figure 3 summarizes the 9,267 comments on 217 papers. Factual errors are rare, 4.8% of the NLP comments and 2.5% of the natural-science comments, so a system spends most of its calls on correct comments and its cost matters. The machine learning reviews have a higher share of errors because they keep only arguments, that is, comments that give reasons for a conclusion. ReviewScore rates the premises of arguments only, so we leave out its claims and questions (Appendix A.1). The median comment has 17, 48, and 70 words, and the median paper has 8.5k, 9.1k, and 14.4k tokens in the NLP, machine learning, and natural-science reviews. A comment is thus short compared with the paper it refers to, so a system that reads the paper for every comment spends almost all of its input on the paper.

4 Method

Overview.

PremiseCheck is a framework that scores a comment cc on a paper DD for the task of §3 in four steps (Figure 4). An LLM decomposes the comment into premises. A decision model routes each premise and then verifies it. The premise scores are aggregated into one comment score. Only the decomposer is an LLM, and it never sees the paper. A decision model ff maps an input text xx and a question aa, phrased as a declarative sentence, to the probability f⁡(x,a)∈[0,1]f(x,a)\in[0,1] that aa holds for xx. Any LLM and any decision model can fill the two roles, and §5 gives the models we use.

Decompose.

The LLM reconstructs the comment as an argument with a conclusion and premises {q1,…,qk}=LLM⁡(c)\{q_{1},\dots,q_{k}\}=\mathrm{LLM}(c), where 1≤k≤61\leq k\leq 6. Each premise is one self-contained declarative sentence that names the method, table, or section it refers to. The prompt asks for both explicit and implicit premises, including what a question presupposes about the paper, and it asks the model not to add facts that the reviewer did not assert or imply (Appendix B.1). The input is only the comment, which averages 24 tokens on the NLP reviews, and the decomposer prompt averages about 256 tokens.

Route.

Some premises are about the paper, such as “the paper does not report results on dataset X.” Others rely on general knowledge, such as “method Y is a standard baseline for this task.” Asking whether such a knowledge premise is true “according to the paper” would wrongly push its probability down. The decision model therefore first estimates the probability ri=f⁡(qi,aroute)r_{i}=f(q_{i},a_{\text{route}}) that premise qiq_{i} can be decided from the paper alone, where aroutea_{\text{route}} is the routing question of Appendix B.2. This routing call receives only the premise, without the paper. With gi=𝟏[ri≥0.5]g_{i}=\mathbf{1}[r_{i}\geq 0.5], premises with gi=1g_{i}=1 are treated as paper-grounded, and the rest as knowledge premises.

Verify.

The decision model then reads the paper together with the premise and answers the question that matches its route,

pi={f⁡((D,qi),apaper)if ​gi=1,f⁡((D,qi),aknow)if ​gi=0,p_{i}=\begin{cases}f\big((D,q_{i}),\,a_{\text{paper}}\big)&\text{if }g_{i}=1,\\ f\big((D,q_{i}),\,a_{\text{know}}\big)&\text{if }g_{i}=0,\end{cases} (2)

where apapera_{\text{paper}} is “The proposition is true according to the paper,” aknowa_{\text{know}} is “The proposition is true,” and the proposition is qiq_{i}. On the natural-science reviews, the decomposer marks which premises to verify in place of routing, and a contradiction question replaces apapera_{\text{paper}} (Appendices B.1 and B.2).

Aggregate.

A comment that rests on a false premise contains a factual error, so the comment score is the lowest premise score,

s⁡(c)=min1≤i≤k⁡pi.s(c)=\min_{1\leq i\leq k}\,p_{i}. (3)

If the decomposer returns no premise, which happens for fewer than 1% of the comments in the NLP reviews, we fall back to the holistic judgment of the decision model.

Why it is cheap.

The cost of PremiseCheck for one comment is that of one LLM call on the comment plus a routing call and a verification call per premise,

C⁡(c)=CLLM​(c)+∑i=1k[Cf​(qi)+Cf​(D,qi)].C(c)=C_{\text{LLM}}(c)+\sum_{i=1}^{k}\big[C_{f}(q_{i})+C_{f}(D,q_{i})\big]. (4)

The LLM call is short because it excludes the paper. A decision model generates no text, so each CfC_{f} grows only with the length of its input, and asking several questions about the same input adds almost no cost. Each verification call reads the paper again, yet in our implementation all decision-model calls together cost $0.0015 per comment on the NLP reviews (Figure 8). In holistic judgment, by contrast, the LLM reads the paper and reasons about it for every comment, so its cost CLLM​(D,c)C_{\text{LLM}}(D,c) grows with the length of the paper at LLM prices.

5 Experimental Setup

Models.

Our implementation of PremiseCheck uses GPT-5.5 as the decomposer and Jev as the decision model, which reads the paper truncated to 24k tokens.11 1 We use gpt-5.5-2026-04-23, gpt-5.4-mini-2026-03-17, and jev-1.13-20260917. The LLMs run with their default sampling and give each probability as an integer from 0 to 100, and Jev is billed only for input tokens, at $0.042 per million. On the machine learning and natural-science reviews, the decomposer uses the prompt variants of Appendix B.1. Our main setting scores each comment on its own, as an assistant would check a comment as soon as the reviewer writes it, before the rest of the review exists. Checking all comments of a finished review together is a different setting, which we evaluate in §8.1. Appendix B.3 gives the prices of the LLMs.

Baselines.

Holistic judgment gives a model the paper and the comment and asks for the probability that the comment’s main criticism is factually correct. We run it with GPT-5.5 at medium, low, and no reasoning, with GPT-5.4-mini, and with Jev. The reference system is holistic GPT-5.5 at medium reasoning. A cascade scores all comments with holistic Jev and sends the 70% it finds most suspicious to holistic GPT-5.5.

Metrics.

We call a system non-inferior to the reference when the lower bound of the 95% interval for the paired AUROC difference, from a bootstrap over papers with 2,000 resamples, is above −3-3, a margin we fixed before running the experiments. Holistic judgment reads the same paper for every comment, so we count its repeated input at the cached price, which favors the baseline.

6 Main Results

6.1 Accuracy, cost, and latency

Table 1 and Figure 5a compare PremiseCheck with holistic judgment and a cascade when each comment is checked on its own. (1) PremiseCheck matches holistic GPT-5.5 at about half the cost. With a medium-reasoning decomposer, it is within 0.3 of the reference or above it on all three parts of ReviewFact, non-inferior on the NLP reviews, and not significantly different on the other two (Appendix C.5). (2) Without reasoning, the cost falls to a quarter on the NLP reviews, where PremiseCheck remains non-inferior (§7.2), while on the other two parts it loses 1.7 to 3.2 points, not significantly. (3) Without reasoning, PremiseCheck takes less than half the time. It needs 45% of the time of holistic GPT-5.5 on the NLP reviews and 37% and 22% on the other parts (Appendix C.3). (4) Cheaper per-comment baselines lose accuracy. Holistic Jev and GPT-5.4-mini fall 5.7 to 13.4 below the reference, holistic GPT-5.5 without reasoning falls 14.0 on the NLP reviews at twice the cost of PremiseCheck, and the cascade costs about three quarters of the reference yet stays below PremiseCheck with the medium-reasoning decomposer on every part.

6.2 Robustness

Figure 6 repeats the comparison with holistic GPT-5.5 on the NLP reviews in two further settings (Appendix C.4). (1) An open-weight decision model works as well. With Kev-27B (Palmer, 2026) as router and verifier, PremiseCheck reaches the same AUROC as with Jev, although with the medium-reasoning decomposer its interval falls just short of non-inferiority. With the no-reasoning decomposer, it is non-inferior at an API cost of 17.8% of the reference, not counting the GPU time of Kev-27B. (2) PremiseCheck is not a proxy for comment length, although longer comments are more often factual errors. Within groups of similar length and after combining each score with length, PremiseCheck stays within 3 points of holistic GPT-5.5 without a significant difference, though none of these comparisons reaches non-inferiority, and adding PremiseCheck to length raises AUROC significantly, by 3.3.

7 What Makes PremiseCheck Work

7.1 Decomposition makes decision models useful

PremiseCheck differs from holistic GPT-5.5 in two ways: it decomposes the comment, and a decision model reads the paper. Figure 8 separates the two by scoring each model as a holistic judge and inside PremiseCheck on the NLP reviews. (1) Decomposition lets a cheap verifier match a frontier LLM. On the same premises, GPT-5.5 as the verifier is no more accurate than Jev but makes the pipeline cost 3.1 times as much as holistic judgment, and the GPT-5.4-mini verifier makes it cost 1.4 times as much as with Jev. (2) Every decision model gains from decomposition. Jev, Kev-27B, Microsoft Decision-1, and Perplexity Decider score 50 to 57 as holistic judges but come within one point of holistic GPT-5.5 as verifiers, although the intervals of Kev-27B and Perplexity Decider fall just short of non-inferiority, whereas the fact-checking model MiniCheck-7B (Tang et al., 2024) falls below its holistic score because it rejects many correct premises (Appendix D.2). (3) Much cheaper LLMs can decompose. With Kev-27B as the verifier, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-5.6 Luna, and Nemotron Super 3 as decomposers are non-inferior to holistic GPT-5.5 at 6% to 17% of the cost of their holistic judgment, while weaker decomposers lose 2 to 6 points.

7.2 Where the savings come from

Figure 8 breaks down the cost on the NLP reviews. (1) The decomposer needs no reasoning. Reasoning makes up about half the cost of holistic GPT-5.5, and without it per-comment holistic judgment falls to chance level on the NLP reviews. PremiseCheck keeps its accuracy there without reasoning, because the LLM only rewrites the comment, while Jev decides whether the paper supports each premise. At low or no reasoning, PremiseCheck is thus more accurate than per-comment holistic judgment on the NLP reviews at less than half its cost. (2) Longer papers yield larger savings. Only Jev reads the paper, so the relative cost of PremiseCheck falls from 53% for the shortest third of the papers to 49% for the longest third.

7.3 Design choices

(1) Routing is needed, but the exact route is not. Kev-27B agrees with Jev on only 65% of the routes yet gives the same AUROC, whereas skipping routing lowers AUROC from 61.8 to 58.8 on a common set of machine learning premises, because knowledge premises then receive low probabilities (Appendix D.5). (2) The weakest premise decides. Taking the mean over premises instead of the minimum lowers AUROC to 59.4, although the mean is slightly better on a label that also counts errors of judgment (Appendix D.5). (3) Contradiction questions add accuracy at no cost. Because Jev is billed only for its input, we ask 16 phrasings of the verification question in one call and average them, eight asking whether the paper supports the premise and eight whether it contradicts the premise (Appendix B.2). Figure 10 shows that AUROC levels off after four phrasings and rises from 63.1 to 65.7 with all 16, a significant gain over the original question. The gain comes from the contradiction questions, since a supporting question also penalizes a premise that the paper does not mention. Without development data on which to select a subset, we keep all 16.

7.4 Error types and scope

(1) PremiseCheck catches both main types of factual error. On Misunderstanding and Neglect, which make up almost all errors in the NLP reviews, PremiseCheck with 16 phrasings scores above holistic GPT-5.5, though not significantly (Appendix D.6). For 79% of the Neglect errors, its lowest premise claims an omission, compared with 36% for correct comments. (2) PremiseCheck targets facts, not judgment. It treats a comment as wrong when one premise is false, which does not hold for errors of judgment. On labels from Phys. Rev. B and ReviewScore that also count unimportant concerns or unreasonable requests, PremiseCheck falls behind holistic GPT-5.5, significantly on Phys. Rev. B and by a wide margin on the few such errors of ReviewScore, but on factual errors alone the gap disappears. Appendix F shows scored comments with their premises.

7.5 Where PremiseCheck fails

Three annotators assign 164 sampled failures to the stage that causes them (Appendix D.7). Figure 10 shows that false alarms come mostly from decomposition on the NLP reviews (58%), where a premise adds to, redirects, or blurs what the reviewer said, and mostly from verification on the natural-science reviews (45%). Holistic GPT-5.5 fails on only 13% and 15% of the machine learning and natural-science false alarms, so these are largely specific to PremiseCheck. Misses on the NLP reviews split between questionable labels (40%) and verification (36%), and holistic GPT-5.5 also fails on 12 of the 20 comments with a questionable label.

8 Using PremiseCheck in Practice

8.1 Batching and fusion

When a review is finished, as for an area chair or an author, all its comments can be checked in one call, as in the original ReviewCritique study (Du et al., 2024). We batch both approaches per review and fuse them by averaging the percentile ranks of their scores. Figure 5b shows these systems, and Appendix E gives the details. (1) Batching helps both approaches. Batched holistic GPT-5.5 without reasoning reaches 67.8 at 7.7% of the reference cost, and batched PremiseCheck reaches 69.0 at 20%. The two do not differ significantly, so holistic GPT-5.5 is the cheaper choice here, while PremiseCheck also returns the premises. (2) Fusion gives the best result. The two scores have a rank correlation of only 0.56, and batched fusion reaches 71.5 at 28% of the reference cost, significantly above batched holistic GPT-5.5.

8.2 Flagging comments for a person to check

A deployed system would flag a few comments for a person to check, each with the premise that Jev finds false. Figure 12 simulates three flagging policies on the NLP reviews, where 4.8% of the comments contain a factual error. (1) Flags of PremiseCheck hit errors two to three times as often as random. This holds for PremiseCheck and batched PremiseCheck among the 5% most suspicious comments, whereas holistic GPT-5.5, per comment or batched, does little better than random despite a similar AUROC. (2) An area chair sees more errors. Reading the three most suspicious comments of each paper finds an error for 40% of the papers that contain one with batched PremiseCheck, compared with 29% with batched holistic GPT-5.5. (3) A flag points to the premise that the paper refutes. In Figure 12, Jev gives the premise that the paper has no summary of its takeaways a probability of 0.04, and the authors reply that each experiment section ends with one. Appendix F.2 explains how we chose this comment and shows a second example and a false alarm.

9 Conclusion

Fact-checking review comments does not require a frontier LLM to read the paper for every comment. ReviewFact labels factual errors in review comments under one definition across three fields. In PremiseCheck, an LLM only rewrites each comment as explicit premises, and a cheap decision model checks them against the paper. When each comment is checked on its own, this division of labor reaches accuracy comparable to GPT-5.5 on every part of ReviewFact at a fraction of its cost. This result does not hinge on one model. Decision models from several providers can verify the premises, and on the NLP reviews, LLMs much cheaper than GPT-5.5, or GPT-5.5 without reasoning, can write them.

PremiseCheck can support peer review at two points. While a reviewer writes, it can check each comment as soon as the comment is written, which is the setting of our main experiments. Once a review is finished, an area chair or an author can check all its comments together, where fusing PremiseCheck with holistic GPT-5.5 gives the best accuracy. In both cases, PremiseCheck is meant to flag a few comments for a person and show the premise that the paper appears to refute, so that the person can check that one claim instead of rereading the paper.

Several directions remain open. Most false alarms on the NLP reviews arise in decomposition, so a decomposer that stays closer to what the reviewer said is a natural next step. Errors of judgment, such as an unimportant concern or an unreasonable request, lie outside PremiseCheck and call for different methods. Finally, ReviewFact can measure future checkers on accuracy, cost, and latency together, and further open-weight decision models can be tested within the same framework.

Limitations

PremiseCheck targets factual errors about the paper, that is, comments that can be checked against what the paper states. A comment can also be wrong in its judgment, for example about the importance of a concern or the novelty of the work (§7.4). Detecting such errors of judgment is a direction for future work.

Our main decision model, Jev, is served through an API. With the open-weight Kev-27B as the decision model, PremiseCheck reaches the same AUROC on the NLP reviews of ReviewFact (§6.2). Testing further open decision models is left for future work.

Ethical Considerations

We use ReviewCritique, ReviewScore, and Phys. Rev. B for research evaluation only. The license of ReviewCritique restricts it to research and evaluation, and we do not train any model on it. We release our code under the MIT license and the NLP and natural-science parts of ReviewFact under the licenses of ReviewCritique and Phys. Rev. B, which allow evaluation but not training. ReviewScore states no license, so for the machine-learning part we release a script that rebuilds it from the original data instead of the data itself. A verifier that wrongly flags a correct comment could unfairly discredit a reviewer, and one that misses an error could lend false authority to a wrong comment. PremiseCheck is meant to direct human attention to comments that may misstate the paper, not to replace the judgment of reviewers, area chairs, or authors.

Appendix Contents

Appendix A Benchmark Details

A.1 Source Annotations

All labels of ReviewFact start from expert judgments in the three source datasets (§3.2).

ReviewCritique (NLP reviews).

In ReviewCritique (Du et al., 2024), 40 members of the NLP community, each with multiple first-authored papers at top NLP venues, label every sentence of a review as reliable or deficient and explain each deficiency. They read the paper, all reviews, the meta-review, and the author rebuttal before labeling. Two of them label each paper independently, and an expert with area-chair experience resolves disagreements. Each labeled unit of a review is one comment in ReviewFact. Deficient comments carry fine-grained error types, four of which are the factual types of ReviewFact. Reliable comments are correct, and deficient comments with one of these four types are errors. We leave out other deficiencies, such as an unconvincing argument, comments that only summarize the paper or list its strengths, and comments of fewer than four words, mostly headers such as “Weaknesses:”.

ReviewScore (machine learning reviews).

In ReviewScore (Ryu et al., 2025), 15 graduate students in AI rate each premise of an automatically reconstructed argument on a five-point factuality scale, and the median of three annotators is the final score. Following ReviewScore, an argument is an error when its lowest premise rating is below 3 and correct when it is above 3. We leave out arguments at exactly 3, as well as claims and questions, which have no premise ratings.

Phys. Rev. B (natural-science reviews).

In Phys. Rev. B (Kim et al., 2026), 45 scientists in the physical, biological, and health sciences judge whether each comment on a Nature-family paper is correct and may add a written rationale. Comments judged correct are correct. Comments judged incorrect are errors only when the error is factual, as decided in Appendix A.2.

A.2 Label Verification

Human verification.

Two of the authors repeat the GPT-5.5 decision of §3.2 on the 178 comments that Phys. Rev. B experts judged incorrect with a rationale. Each annotator sees the comment, the expert rationale, and the paper text, but not the GPT-5.5 label, and the two annotators see the comments in different random orders. The guidelines in Figure 13 define the three labels with the error types of ReviewCritique. Table 3 reports the agreement. Of the 38 comments with different labels, 17 are labeled factual by one annotator and judgment by the other, and 21 involve the unclear label.

Results with human labels.

Table 3 scores the natural-science reviews with the labels of the annotators in place of the GPT-5.5 labels on these 178 comments. As with the GPT-5.5 labels, comments labeled judgment or unclear are left out. The difference between PremiseCheck and holistic GPT-5.5 ranges from −3.7-3.7 to +2.7+2.7, and no interval excludes zero. PremiseCheck is 2.7 above holistic GPT-5.5 on the 47 errors that both annotators label factual.

Automatic labels.

GPT-5.5 at medium reasoning labels these comments with the following system prompt. The prompt uses the definitions of Figure 13 but shows only the comment and the expert rationale, not the paper. The user message gives the comment, the rationale of the primary Phys. Rev. B expert, and the rationale of a second expert when that expert also judged the comment incorrect.

⬇
You classify why an expert judged a peer-review comment on a scientific paper to be incorrect.
You receive one review comment and the rationale of the expert annotator who judged it Not Correct (and, if a second annotator also judged it Not Correct, that annotator’s rationale). You do not see the paper. Decide from the comment and the rationale alone.
Choose exactly one label:
- "factual": the comment says something about THIS paper that the paper does not support. Give one subtype:
- "Misunderstanding": the comment misreads what the paper does or claims.
- "Neglect": the comment says the paper lacks something that it clearly contains (an experiment, a detail, a discussion).
- "Unstated statement": the comment asserts something about the paper that has no basis in it.
- "Inaccurate Summary": the comment misstates the content or contribution of the paper.
- "judgment": the comment is wrong in its judgment, not its facts, for example about importance, scope or novelty, an unreasonable request, being too harsh or overstated, or a disagreement about field knowledge.
- "unclear": the rationale does not let you decide.
Rules:
- An error about a cited paper rather than this paper is "judgment".
- When the rationale mainly says the comment is too harsh or overstated but also mentions the paper’s content, choose "judgment".
- Give the subtype only for "factual"; otherwise use null.
- Give a one-sentence reason.
Return ONLY JSON: {"label": "...", "subtype": "..." or null, "reason": "..."}

Appendix B Implementation Details

B.1 Prompts

Decomposition prompt.

On the NLP reviews, the decomposer uses the following system prompt, and the user message is the review comment.

⬇
You reconstruct ONE peer-review item as an argument, so that each step can be fact-checked separately.
List the premises the item relies on, explicit and implicit, and its conclusion.
- Each premise is ONE self-contained declarative sentence that is either true or false.
- Write it so it can be understood without the review item: say "the paper", and name the method, dataset, table, figure or equation it is about.
- Include premises about what the paper states, reports, shows or omits, and the general-knowledge premises that the reasoning needs.
- Keep each premise as close to the reviewer’s own claim as possible. Do not add facts the reviewer did not assert or imply. Do not judge whether a premise is true.
- If the item is a question, write the presuppositions of the question as premises (for example what the reviewer assumes the paper does or does not state).
- Use 1 to 6 premises.
Return ONLY JSON: {"premises": ["...", "..."], "conclusion": "..."}

Variant for the machine learning reviews.

On the machine learning reviews, the decomposer keeps fewer premises.

⬇
You reconstruct ONE peer-review item as a short argument, so that each step can be fact-checked separately.
List ONLY the premises the reviewer actually asserts or directly presupposes, in the reviewer’s own terms:
- the reviewer’s claims about what the paper states, reports, shows or omits;
- at most ONE general-knowledge premise, and only if the reviewer’s conclusion depends on it.
Each premise is ONE self-contained declarative sentence: say "the paper" and name the method, dataset, table, figure or equation it is about.
Do NOT describe the paper beyond what the reviewer says. Do NOT add background facts, assumptions or inferences of your own. Do not judge whether a premise is true.
If the item is a question, write only what the question presupposes about the paper.
Use 1 to 4 premises.
Return ONLY JSON: {"premises": ["...", "..."], "conclusion": "..."}

Variant for the natural-science reviews.

On the natural-science reviews, the decomposer labels each premise as paper, knowledge, or opinion. Only paper premises are verified, or all premises when none is labeled paper.

⬇
You reconstruct ONE peer-review item as a short argument, so that each step can be fact-checked separately.
List the premises the reviewer asserts or directly presupposes, and give each premise a type:
- "paper": a claim about what the paper states, reports, shows, cites or omits.
- "knowledge": a factual claim about the world or about other work that does not depend on this paper (for example what a standard method does, or what another paper introduced).
- "opinion": an evaluation, norm or recommendation (for example "X is limited", "Y is unconvincing", "the paper should do Z", "a good paper would ...").
Rules:
- Each premise is ONE self-contained declarative sentence. Say "the paper" and name the method, dataset, table, figure, section or equation it is about.
- Make "paper" and "knowledge" premises concrete and checkable. Do not use vague or evaluative words in them (little, limited, clearly, severe, sufficient, convincing, well). Put such evaluations in "opinion" premises.
- For an omission, state exactly what is missing (for example "The paper does not report results on dataset D"), not how much is missing.
- Keep each premise as close to the reviewer’s own claim as possible. Do not add facts the reviewer did not assert or imply. Do not describe the paper beyond what the reviewer says. Do not judge whether a premise is true.
- If the item is a question, write only what the question presupposes about the paper.
- Use 1 to 5 premises in total.
Return ONLY JSON: {"premises": [{"text": "...", "type": "paper"}, ...], "conclusion": "..."}

LLM judge prompt.

Holistic GPT-5.5, holistic GPT-5.4-mini, and the LLM verifiers on paper-grounded premises use the following system prompt.

⬇
You judge whether statements are true according to a given evidence text from a scientific paper. Judge each statement only from the evidence text. For each statement, give the probability (integer 0-100) that it is true according to the evidence. Return ONLY JSON: {"p": {"<id>": <int>, ...}}.

For knowledge premises, the LLM verifiers use a neutral prompt that allows general knowledge.

B.2 Decision-Model Questions

Questions per step.

Table 4 lists the questions for Jev. On the natural-science reviews, the contradiction question replaces the paper-grounded question, and we use one minus its probability.

Phrasings of the verification question.

Table 5 lists the 16 phrasings of §7.3, which go into a single Jev call per premise. Paper-grounded premises use the left column and knowledge premises the right column. The random subsets of Figure 10 take the ii-th phrasings of both columns together.

B.3 Paper Input, Cost, and Latency

Paper input.

On the NLP reviews, all LLM systems see the same paper as Jev, truncated to 24k tokens. On the natural-science reviews, holistic GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.4-mini read the full paper with the judgment prompt of Phys. Rev. B.

Cost.

Cost converts the token usage of each call into dollars at public list prices. GPT-5.5 costs $5.00 per million input tokens, $0.50 per million cached input tokens, and $30.00 per million output tokens, with reasoning tokens billed as output. GPT-5.4-mini costs $0.75, $0.075, and $4.50 for the same three categories. For Jev we use the cost reported by the API. Kev-27B runs on our own GPUs, so we report its GPU time in addition to the API cost of the decomposer. We report cost per comment and as a percentage of the reference.

Latency.

Latency is the mean wall-clock time to score one comment. We measure it from the recorded API calls, with the premises of one comment checked in parallel. On the natural-science reviews, we average over 300 random comments.

C.5 Machine Learning and Natural-Science Reviews

Table 10 gives the results on the machine learning and natural-science reviews and compares decomposition prompts and verification questions on them. On the machine learning reviews, the machine learning prompt yields a shorter premise list. It leaves out premises that the reviewer did not state and so reduces false alarms on correct comments. On the natural-science reviews, the choice of verification question matters most. Asking whether the paper supports a premise treats details that the paper does not mention as false. Asking whether the paper contradicts the premise avoids this.

Appendix D Additional Analysis

This section gives the full numbers behind §7.

D.1 Capability Map of the Decision Model

Table 11 measures Jev on individual operations of review verification, and Figure 14 plots the results. For each operation, Jev, GPT-5.4-mini (low reasoning), and GPT-5.5 (medium reasoning) receive the same input and questions, and the two LLMs return a probability as an integer from 0 to 100. Premise checking and routing use ReviewScore (Ryu et al., 2025): 452 human-reconstructed premises about the paper, 33 of them false, and the grounding source annotators gave for 972 premises. Comment-type classification uses ReviewScore comments. Duplicate detection and all judgments use Phys. Rev. B (Kim et al., 2026).

On the operations that PremiseCheck uses, Jev is as accurate as GPT-5.5: it checks a single premise against the full paper at least as well, and it routes premises equally well. On classifying the type of a comment, it is significantly better at recognizing arguments but significantly worse at recognizing claims and questions. On judgments about a whole comment, Jev falls behind, and on whether a comment is correct, all models are close to chance. A premise check that reads the full paper costs $0.00044 with Jev, and its median latency is 216 ms compared with 5.1 s for GPT-5.5.

D.2 Verifiers

Table 12 gives the AUROC of each model as a holistic judge and as the verifier of PremiseCheck, together with the paired differences and the latency, and Table 13 adds MiniCheck. As a holistic judge, Kev-27B differs from holistic GPT-5.5 by −8.9-8.9 [−11.8-11.8, −6.0-6.0].

Off-the-shelf fact-checking models.

We replace Jev with MiniCheck (Tang et al., 2024), a family of small models trained to test whether a document supports a claim. The main variant is Bespoke-MiniCheck-7B (MiniCheck-7B), and we also run MiniCheck-Flan-T5-Large (MiniCheck-T5). Both read the same truncated paper as Jev and use the default chunking and aggregation of the MiniCheck library. The premises are those of PremiseCheck with the medium-reasoning and the no-reasoning decomposer, and the comment score is again the minimum over premises. MiniCheck takes no question, so every premise is checked against the paper. In the hybrid variant, Jev checks the knowledge premises instead. GPU time is the wall-clock time of each stage on eight H200 GPUs divided by the number of comments, as for Kev-27B. Table 13 gives the results.

MiniCheck-7B lowers PremiseCheck from 63.0 to 54.0, and MiniCheck-T5 behaves the same. The cause is false alarms on correct premises. Among premises that do not claim an omission, MiniCheck-7B gives 25.5% a probability below 0.3, compared with 11.2% for Jev. A comment has 3.3 premises on average, so with the minimum a single false alarm marks the whole comment as wrong. Using Jev for the knowledge premises recovers only 2.8, so most of the gap lies on premises that are checked against the paper.

Holistic MiniCheck-7B, which scores the whole comment against the paper, reaches 59.5 at no API cost. PremiseCheck with a single question is +3.4+3.4 [−0.0-0.0, +6.9+6.9] above it. With the 16 phrasings per premise of §7.3, PremiseCheck is +6.1+6.1 [+3.0+3.0, +9.0+9.0] above it.

D.3 Cost Breakdown and Paper Length

Table 15 gives the per-comment costs on the NLP reviews behind Figure 8. The first block splits the cost of holistic GPT-5.5 and of the GPT-5.5 decomposer by token type. At medium reasoning, holistic judgment reads on average 9,991 input tokens per comment, of which 8,831 hit the prompt cache, and produces 383 output tokens, of which 353 are reasoning tokens. The decomposer reads only the comment.

The second block gives the cost of the two stages of PremiseCheck, the decomposer and Jev. Jev costs $0.0015 per comment with the low- and no-reasoning decomposers as well. The GPT-5.4-mini and GPT-5.5 rows give the cost of the verifiers that replace Jev in §7.1. The last block gives the saving of PremiseCheck with the no-reasoning decomposer over holistic GPT-5.5 at medium and at low reasoning.

Table 15 gives the cost per comment by paper length behind Figure 8.

D.4 Other Decision Models and Other LLMs

Table 16 gives the full results of §7.1. The decision models receive the same requests as Jev through the same API, and all other settings follow §5. The LLMs receive the decomposition and holistic prompts of GPT-5.5 unchanged. GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-5.6 Luna use medium reasoning, like GPT-5.5. The other LLMs do not reason and use temperature 0, except Nemotron Super 3, which uses its default sampling because it produces malformed output at temperature 0. A holistic answer from which no probability can be read is scored 0.5, which affects 2.1% of the comments for Nemotron Super 3, 0.6% for Ministral 3 14B, and fewer than 0.1% for the other LLMs. API costs use public prices, and Kev-27B runs on our own GPUs, so its checks add no API cost.

D.7 Failure Analysis

§7.5 analyzes where PremiseCheck fails. For each part of ReviewFact, we sample false alarms, which are correct comments among the 10% lowest PremiseCheck scores of that part, and misses, which are factual errors scored above the median, with a fixed seed. The targets are 50 of each on the NLP reviews, 15 of each on the machine learning reviews, and 20 of each on the natural-science reviews, where only 14 misses qualify and we take all of them. Each annotator sees the comment, the expert label and rationale, the premises with their types, routes, and probabilities, and the paper text that Jev reads, and assigns the earliest stage that explains the failure with one code of Table 22. Three annotators label all 164 comments independently. Fleiss’ κ\kappa is 0.45 for the stage and 0.47 for the code. We take the code chosen by at least two annotators and settle the other 26 comments by discussion. A comment counts as a failure of holistic GPT-5.5 under the same rule when GPT-5.5 scores a correct comment within its own lowest 10% or a factual error above its own median. Table 22 gives the counts behind Figure 10.

Figure 16 shows one case for each stage, chosen by a fixed rule: among comments whose final code was chosen by at least two annotators, all of them with the highest confidence, we take the shortest comment. No aggregation failure meets this rule.

Appendix E Batching and Fusion

Table 23 compares per-comment and batched systems and their fusion. Batched holistic judgment uses the prompt and question of holistic GPT-5.5, with all comments of one review numbered in the evidence and one question per comment. Batched PremiseCheck uses the decomposition prompt of Appendix B.1, changed only so that it returns one premise list per numbered comment. Both batched systems see the same comments of each review. When an answer misses comments, we ask once more for the missing ones, after which no comment remained missing. The cost of one call is divided evenly among the comments of the review. In the row “Jev batched”, Jev also reads the paper once for up to eight premises, with two questions per premise. Latency is per comment, computed as the time for the whole review divided by its number of comments.

Appendix F Examples

F.1 Scored Comments

Figure 17 shows two comments from the NLP reviews with the premises of PremiseCheck (medium-reasoning decomposer) and the probabilities that Jev assigns to them.

The first comment is a factual error. We drew it at random from short factual errors in human-written reviews that both systems flag, that is, errors in the lowest 10% of PremiseCheck scores that holistic GPT-5.5 also scores at or below its median. The reviewer claims that the motivation of the paper is unclear. The expert disagrees, because the authors state a motivation for their analysis. PremiseCheck splits the comment into two premises. Jev checks the second premise, that the paper does not make its motivation clear, against the paper and gives it a probability of 0.04. This premise states the point that the expert disputes, and it sets the comment score. Holistic GPT-5.5 also flags the comment, with a probability of 0.15.

The second comment is correct, but PremiseCheck flags it. We drew it at random from short correct comments of human-written reviews in the lowest 10% of PremiseCheck scores. The comment describes evidence from representational similarity analysis and linear mappings, but the paper text contains neither. The comment therefore likely refers to another paper. The decomposer rewrote “paper” as “the paper”, so premises 1 and 2 are false as written, and Jev gives both a probability of 0.03. Holistic GPT-5.5 also gives the comment a very low score.

Figure 18 shows a further factual error, for which PremiseCheck gives a much lower score than holistic Jev. We chose it among NLP factual errors with a PremiseCheck score at or below 0.10 and a holistic Jev score at or above 0.60. The comment implies that the paper does not test other large-scale language models such as OPT and GPT-3.

F.2 Flagged Comments with Author Responses

We choose the examples by a fixed rule among the 10% of machine learning comments that PremiseCheck finds most suspicious. The two caught errors are the shortest comments that the ReviewScore annotators label as misinformed and whose authors reply that the paper contains what the comment asks for. Example 1 is Figure 12, and Example 2 in Figure 19 is the second. The false alarm is the shortest comment that the annotators label as correct and whose authors accept it. In Example 3, the reviewer says that Section 1 does not cite CLIP, and the authors confirm this by adding the citation. Jev still gives the premise a probability of 0.04, probably because the paper cites CLIP in Section 4 and Jev reads the whole paper, so it cannot tell in which section a citation appears.
